sections.html:
South of Richmond, Chesterfield County is bounded largely by the James River on the north and the Appomattox on the south. Chesterfield Court House is the seat, and no towns are incorporated here. Residents numbered 364,548 in 2020, and the county puts its 2025 estimate at 397,148. It covers 437 square miles, 423 of them land.

The postwar boom made this a commuter suburb of Richmond, which means many of its houses are decades old. Original roofs, tired heating and cooling equipment and dated kitchens often keep a house on the market, and a mortgage buyer may demand repairs that a cash buyer in present condition would not.

Values are redone yearly here. Notices go out by February 1 showing the January 1 value, and the county holds that assessments must equal 100 percent of fair market value. The Board of Supervisors sets the rate, which the county lists as $0.89 per $100 of assessed value for 2026. Values rest on inspections, sales data and comparisons with similar nearby properties.

StepDate
Assessment notices mailedBy February 1
Value dateJanuary 1
Appeal to Real Estate AssessmentsMarch 15
Appeal to the Board of EqualizationApril 15
Commercial income and expense surveyJuly 15

Your first filing goes to Real Estate Assessments and is due March 15. Still disagree? The Board of Equalization takes appeals until April 15. Late applications are never processed, and you cannot appeal further without using the first level.

  1. Review your values on the county's READ site or contact the office.
  2. Get the application and file a separate one for each property.
  3. Attach support: up to three comparable properties, a recent appraisal or photos, and for income property three years of income and expense statements plus a current rent roll.
  4. If a representative files for you, add a notarized Letter of Authorization.
  5. An appraiser may ask questions or inspect, then tells you the outcome.

State code makes the Board of Equalization independent: a Circuit Court judge appoints its members and the Virginia Department of Taxation trains them. Section 58.1-3379 starts from the assumption that the assessor is right, so you must supply evidence to the contrary. Real Estate Assessments is at 6801 Mimms Loop, phone 804-748-1321, email assessor@chesterfield.gov.

Where a parcel sits decides who serves it and bills it. Ettrick shows the problem: most of it uses a Petersburg mailing address, yet it is in Chesterfield County. A seller there should confirm with the county tax office, and not the postal city, which locality charges the tax.

Real Estate Assessments also names a contact for the Lower Magnolia Green Community Development Authority. Have the closing agent check whether your parcel falls in a special district or owes a charge beyond the regular county bill.

  • Automated Payment Service: free, with taxes debited on the due date after about 30 to 45 days of activation.
  • APS returns: a $50 return-item fee applies for insufficient funds, on top of any bank fees.
  • Citizen Portal: shows invoices for the most recent six years.
  • Payment kiosks: take cash, cards and checks around the clock.

Heirs sorting out an old account can use the six-year view to see what was billed. The Treasurer can explain anything older.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The tax now due falls on Monday, December 7, 2026, and missing it brings a 10 percent penalty. Visit the Treasurer's Office at 9901 Lori Road, Room 101, Chesterfield, VA 23832, or write to P.O. Box 70. The phone, 804-748-1201, is answered weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

  • Online through the Citizen Portal, which now requires an account.
  • By phone at 855-933-5661, around the clock.
  • Using your own bank's bill-pay service, which mails to P.O. Box 70.
  • At one of the payment kiosks in seven library and administration buildings.
  • By the Lane B. Ramsey Administration Building drop box, with checks or money orders only.

Credit cards carry a 2 percent processor fee and debit cards a flat $2.50, while eCheck has no fee. State code in 58.1-3916 caps interest at 10 percent a year and the property penalty at 10 percent.

sections.h2: What to gather before you appeal
sections.html:
Pull the county record for your parcel first and compare every line with the house: floor area, room counts, any outbuildings. Next, assemble up to three comparable properties, a current appraisal if you hold one, and photos showing trouble spots like a worn roof or a cracked foundation. One application covers one parcel, so an owner of two lots files twice.

Set a calendar reminder for March 15, because the county will not process a late application and the first level must be completed before the board. If someone else files for you, get the notarized authorization signed early. An appraiser may call with questions or ask to inspect, so be ready to explain what you see in the house that the record does not show.

sections.h2: If your tax bill is behind
sections.html:
Owners short on cash by the due date may apply to the county for a payment plan. Interest and fees continue during the plan, staff reply within two business days, and approval is not promised.

A plan also leaves a DMV stop in place until accounts are paid in full, which matters if you owe both vehicle and real estate tax.

sections.h2: A cash sale in Chesterfield County
sections.html:
Owners choose cash when a house is tired, an heir lives out of state or a tax or loan balance is growing. Because most Chesterfield houses are postwar and later subdivisions, repairs such as roofs and heating and cooling equipment are common and can stall a financed sale. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it is removes the repair negotiation and shortens the timeline.

Before you take any offer, put your own numbers beside it: the January 1 value on your notice, the tax you owe, and what repairs would realistically cost. An offer that is clear about closing costs and the payoff of any open balance is one you can compare with a listing price on equal terms. Ask for the offer in writing, and ask when funds would reach you.

The deed carries a grantor tax of fifty cents per $500 under 58.1-802. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure that matches your closing date, since interest grows daily. Cash Home Buyers can buy a Chesterfield County house as is, including one with back tax or repairs, and settle the payoff from the proceeds.

A county this size means many owners manage a house from far away. An heir or an owner who moved should request the Treasurer's balance early, because statements keep arriving at the old address while a balance grows.

faqs.q: What is the Chesterfield County real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: The county lists $0.89 per $100 of assessed value for 2026, set by the Board of Supervisors.

faqs.q: When do I have to appeal a Chesterfield assessment?
faqs.a: March 15 for Real Estate Assessments and April 15 for the Board of Equalization. The county processes no late applications.

faqs.q: Where is the Chesterfield County Treasurer?
faqs.a: At 9901 Lori Road, Room 101, Chesterfield, VA 23832. Call 804-748-1201 on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 5 p.m.

faqs.q: Does a Chesterfield payment plan stop penalties?
faqs.a: No. Interest and fees keep accruing during a plan, and a plan does not release a DMV stop.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Chesterfield County house with back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, the balance is normally paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure before the closing date.
